'''Julia Parrish''' is an ecologist and conservation biologist at the [[University of Washington]] known for her research on seabirds and for her leadership in [[citizen science]]. She is an elected fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]].

== Education and career ==
Parrish has an undergraduate degree from Carnegie-Mellon (1982)<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|last=Wagner|first=Eric|date=June 15, 2010|title=The Value of Dead Bird Watching|url=https://psmag.com/environment/the-value-of-dead-bird-watching-16756|access-date=2021-10-01|website=Pacific Standard|language=en}}</ref> where she studied biochemistry and [[biophysics]]. While she was an undergraduate student, she spent a period of time at the [[Duke University Marine Laboratory]], which she credits for guiding her towards getting her Ph.D. at Duke University studying the schooling behavior of fish.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|title=Julia K. Parrish {{!}} UW Biology|url=https://www.biology.washington.edu/people/profile/julia-k-parrish|access-date=2021-10-01|website=www.biology.washington.edu|language=en}}</ref> Parrish moved to the [[University of Washington]]{{When|date=October 2021}} where she holds the Lowell A. and Frankie L. Wakefield Endowed Professorship.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Julia Parrish|url=https://environment.uw.edu/faculty/julia-parrish|access-date=2021-10-06|website=College of the Environment|language=en-US}}</ref>

== Research ==
Parrish's research is a combination of observational research and conservation activities. Her graduate research centered on fish where she examined mucus production by the [[Atlantic silverside]] fish<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Parrish|first1=J. K.|last2=Kroen|first2=W. K.|date=1988|title=Sloughed mucus and drag-reduction in a school of Atlantic silversides, Menidia menidia|url=https://link.springer.com/10.1007/BF00391298|journal=Marine Biology|language=en|volume=97|issue=2|pages=165–169|doi=10.1007/BF00391298|bibcode=1988MarBi..97..165P |s2cid=84320189|issn=0025-3162|url-access=subscription}}</ref> and the importance of physical location within [[Shoaling and schooling|schooling]] groups of fish.<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Parrish|first=Julia K.|date=1989|title=Re-examining the selfish herd: are central fish safer?|url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0003347289801435|journal=Animal Behaviour|language=en|volume=38|issue=6|pages=1048–1053|doi=10.1016/S0003-3472(89)80143-5|s2cid=53148279|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last=Parrish|first=Julia K.|date=1989|title=Layering with depth in a heterospecific fish aggregation|url=https://link.springer.com/10.1007/BF00001024|journal=Environmental Biology of Fishes|language=en|volume=26|issue=2|pages=79–85|doi=10.1007/BF00001024|bibcode=1989EnvBF..26...79P |s2cid=40434181|issn=0378-1909|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Parrish began working on [[Tatoosh Island, Washington|Tatoosh Island]] in 1990 after an invitation to the island from a graduate student in [[Robert T. Paine (zoologist)|Bob Paine]]'s lab.<ref name=":2">{{Cite web|last=LYKE|first=M. L.|date=2001-09-11|title=Murre-maid of Tatoosh|url=https://www.seattlepi.com/lifestyle/article/Murre-maid-of-Tatoosh-1065304.php|access-date=2021-10-01|website=seattlepi.com|language=en-US}}</ref> Her work on the island focuses on [[common murre]]s,<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Parrish|first=Julia K.|date=1995|title=Influence of Group Size and Habitat Type on Reproductive Success in Common Murres (Uria aalge)|journal=The Auk|volume=112|issue=2|pages=390–401|doi=10.2307/4088726|jstor=4088726|issn=0004-8038|doi-access=free}}</ref> a seabird that forms dense nesting colonies on the island.<ref name=":2" /> She has examined  interactions between [[bald eagle]]s and common murres and noted declines in the common murre population as a result of the recovery of the bald eagles.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Parrish|first1=Julia K.|last2=Marvier|first2=Michelle|last3=Paine|first3=Robert T.|title=Direct and Indirect Effects: Interactions Between Bald Eagles and Common Murres|date=2001|url=http://doi.wiley.com/10.1890/1051-0761(2001)011[1858:DAIEIB]2.0.CO;2|journal=Ecological Applications|language=en|volume=11|issue=6|pages=1858–1869|doi=10.1890/1051-0761(2001)011[1858:DAIEIB]2.0.CO;2|issn=1051-0761|url-access=subscription}}</ref> Parrish has modeled the role of aggregating animals in the survival of organisms<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Parrish|first=J. K.|date=1999-04-02|title=Complexity, Pattern, and Evolutionary Trade-Offs in Animal Aggregation|url=https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.284.5411.99|journal=Science|volume=284|issue=5411|pages=99–101|doi=10.1126/science.284.5411.99|pmid=10102827|bibcode=1999Sci...284...99P|url-access=subscription}}</ref><ref>{{Cite == Citizen science ==
[[File:Common_Murre_COASST_.jpg|alt=Picture of dead bird|thumb|A common murre carcass found along the high wrack being prepared for photographic identification by COASST volunteers]]
Parrish founded and directs the Coastal Observation and Seabird Survey Team, [[COASST]], a citizen science project started in 1999 that organizes volunteers to gather details about dead birds and [[marine debris]] on beaches along the west coast of the United States.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Our Story – COASST|url=https://coasst.org/about/our-story/|access-date=2021-10-06|language=en-US}}</ref><ref name=":1" /> Parrish's activities include research into the scale of citizen science projects, the value of in-kind contributions made by volunteers,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Theobald|first1=E. J.|last2=Ettinger|first2=A. K.|last3=Burgess|first3=H. K.|last4=DeBey|first4=L. B.|last5=Schmidt|first5=N. R.|last6=Froehlich|first6=H. E.|last7=Wagner|first7=C.|last8=HilleRisLambers|first8=J.|last9=Tewksbury|first9=J.|last10=Harsch|first10=M. A.|last11=Parrish|first11=J. K.|date=2015-01-01|title=Global change and local solutions: Tapping the unrealized potential of citizen science for biodiversity research|journal=Biological Conservation|language=en|volume=181|pages=236–244|doi=10.1016/j.biocon.2014.10.021|issn=0006-3207|doi-access=free|bibcode=2015BCons.181..236T }}</ref> factors limiting the use of data collected by citizen scientists,<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Burgess|first1=H. K.|last2=DeBey|first2=L. B.|last3=Froehlich|first3=H. E.|last4=Schmidt|first4=N.|last5=Theobald|first5=E. J.|last6=Ettinger|first6=A. K.|last7=HilleRisLambers|first7=J.|last8=Tewksbury|first8=J.|last9=Parrish|first9=J. K.|date=2017-04-01|title=The science of citizen science: Exploring barriers to use as a primary research tool|journal=Biological Conservation|series=The role of citizen science in biological conservation|language=en|volume=208|pages=113–120|doi=10.1016/j.biocon.2016.05.014|issn=0006-3207|doi-access=free|bibcode=2017BCons.208..113B }}</ref> and demographic factors leading to the success of data collection by citizen science projects.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Parrish|first1=Julia K.|last2=Jones|first2=Timothy|last3=Burgess|first3=Hillary K.|last4=He|first4=Yurong|last5=Fortson|first5=Lucy|last6=Cavalier|first6=Darlene|date=2019-02-05|title=Hoping for optimality or designing for inclusion: Persistence, learning, and the social network of citizen science|journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences|language=en|volume=116|issue=6|pages=1894–1901|doi=10.1073/pnas.1807186115|issn=0027-8424|pmc=6369789|pmid=30718390|bibcode=2019PNAS..116.1894P|doi-access=free}}</ref>
